The arguments here around intent are (potentially) irrelevant. Case law is clear that setting up a situation which foreseeably highly likely to produce an outcome (gross negligence) is (more or less and it's not quite this simple and varies by offense) equivalent to intent. In fact, automating something is often treated more harshly under the law than just doing it yourself.

United States v. Morris (1991)

Robert Morris released a self-propagating computer worm that caused widespread disruption. The Second Circuit upheld his conviction under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act even though the government hadn't proven that he intended the resulting damage.

People v. Ceballos (1974)

Ceballos rigged a rifle to fire if someone opened his garage door. The California Supreme Court reviewed the principle that someone who installs a dangerous mechanical device may be held responsible for its consequences as though they had personally inflicted the injury. Ceballos was convicted of assault with a deadly weapon, and the California Supreme Court unanimously upheld his conviction in 1974.

Sizing the steps matter. Disclaimer up front: we are all figuring it out as we go along, there are no hard and fast rules that fully generalize. You just need to try and develop your own feel for it.

In my case, for some types of work - which sound similar to things you mention - I started slowing AI down intentionally. Software development, if it's something simple/common and thus "in-distribution", LLMs can zero-shot complex projects just fine. But in more R&D work, I found that errors crop up quickly and accumulate, and end result of "go and just make X" is usually bad.

Now, the problem I found with usual workflows for this kind of work is, agents race ahead and very quickly, I can't keep up anymore. So I reworked my workflow to make AI work in small steps optimized strictly for maximizing my ability to validate the outcome, and minimize time I spend doing it. So now, the thing (say diagnosing a performance regression of some complex codebase run on a cluster) may take me a whole day, where "unchained", agentic swarm would do it in 30-60 minutes - but, at the end of the day, my method is near 100% guaranteed to be correct, with every intermediate step vouched and reusable for future work, whereas "agentic swarm" approach, that hour of work, 90% of the times I'd just skim and throw away and reprompt, because I couldn't even begin to guess which part is correct, which isn't, so in the end, it was just a fast way to waste lots of tokens.

I see many people have complex systems involving skills, agent swarms with roles, agent factories, 20 termux panes and whatnot. Maybe that's the way, I don't know. Nobody knows. But it's not necessary to start getting value from LLMs. I therefore recommend my "lazy person's basic approach":

- Throw a task at LLM

- Check result, see what you like or not like about it

- If you just can't keep up, ask it to do smaller steps; if you don't understand, ask it to explain

- Just do that a lot, and don't be afraid to make both absurdly large and absurdly small asks

- You'll quickly get a feel for where AI can help you, and where it's not yet worth the time handholding it

OEMs have been required to stop doing most of the non-standard things they were doing in relation to this and it's not hard for app developers to deal with anymore unless they care about it on end-of-life Android versions.

The persistent notification for foreground services is mandatory for apps to implement but entirely optional for users. The notification channel can simply be toggled off to hide it. Apps are required to make a notification for each foreground service to provide transparency. It gives apps a way to explain why they're doing it to end users and the notification be toggled off if the user doesn't want it. It can also be kept enabled but collapsed at the bottom with no lockscreen or status bar display. Apps are required to use at least low importance themselves so the user needs to opt in to collapsing and hiding it or turning it off.

Fully open source apps can use UnifiedPush as the Molly fork of Signal does instead of their own push connection. Similarly to FCM, UnifiedPush providers can provide reliable and efficient push messaging including push notifications. Unlike FCM, users can choose the local implementation and the service providing it including the option to self-host it. There are multiple options available as an existing service. There are a growing number of apps supporting UnifiedPush.

Signal's own fallback push messaging for push notifications when FCM isn't present is very inefficient. It substantially reduces battery life even if it's the only app doing push with another mechanism. Molly's UnifiedPush support works much better.

Using a single push messaging connection or at least only a couple (FCM and UnifiedPush) is definitely far more efficient than using dozens. Using many push messaging connections will drain a lot of power due to each needing to be maintained with regular checks which will typically not align well. Having many causes a drastically higher number of wakes from sleep and non-idle time. That's especially true if the push messaging connections aren't implemented very efficiently. Even a single inefficient one can drain a lot of power. Signal's fallback isn't as bad as it used to be but it's not efficient.

In general, in my experience, grep is better than almost anything else you can use. It's very very fast and efficient, very flexible, and does not require any indexing pass, is never out of date, and doesn't require you to guess ahead of time what files you might want to search or how to process search tokens.

"Search your files, repos and agent sessions, locally, and give your agents the best context for the job. One search points them to the few passages that matter, instead of grepping the whole disk."

Grep is already searching for relevant passages with a single tool call. This is clearly LLM written copy. It makes literally no sense.

This reminds me of the dating app advert I keep seeing on tiktok, which says that other dating sites "force you to be the loudest voice on your profile". There's no interpretation that makes sense, it's just the typical LLM gibberish.

Indexing local files makes search faster (in theory, but in practice maybe not for less than a few tens of GB of local files on fast SSD), but not more flexible or requiring less tool calls.

It also will always suffer from being a little behind the on disk state, which is terrible when you are trying to do something like find all the references to something under active development, or when changing branches. Consider you checkout a branch and call this tool, it will just lie to you, telling your LLM there are matches in files that no longer match, getting line numbers wrong, missing matches in other files. Every time you change branches it will go nuts trying to reindex everything. The best case scenario is still probably performance on par with grep but out of date and doing a ton of extra work to index files whether or not you ever need to search them.

Grep can take general regex, which more or less can't be indexed, so there's very few things that are more flexible or produce less tool calls than grep.

Grep is also absurdly fast, if you don't know how fast it is it's faster than you think. Here I use ripgrep to search every piece of code I have checked out, around 11GB of data (more or less) in 0.2s (regular gnu grep takes 4s, mostly because it doesn't exclude .git/ folders and only uses one processor):

For human-maintained code you manage duplication and locality of changes in the codebase because you want concepts to fit inside a human’s working memory. Keeping method bodies short is so they fit in one code window on the screen.
